title: Nicholas of Myra
hook: a bishop who, the story goes, dropped gold through a poor family's window by night

segments.voice: Yesterday, Athanasius, who ran and hid but wouldn't change the word. Your line: against the world.

A bag lands on the floor in the dark. It came through the window, and inside there's gold. A bishop named Nicholas, in Myra, a town near the southern coast of what's now Turkey. The red coat, the sleigh and the reindeer come much later, and from somewhere else. Before any of that, there's a family in trouble, a window, and a man who very much didn't want to be thanked. We know little about Nicholas from records of his own time. Mostly we have the story people told about him, and the way his church remembered him.

The old Lives of Nicholas tell it this way. A man in Nicholas's town had been well off and lost everything. He had three daughters, and no money for their dowries, which meant no marriages. The story says he was close to a terrible choice: letting his daughters be sold into shame to keep the household alive. Nicholas heard. He didn't knock, call a meeting or make a speech. At night he threw a bag of gold through the window, and left. The father found it and wept, and the first daughter was married. Nicholas came back another night and did it again. On the third night, the father was waiting. He ran after the shadow in the street, caught up, and fell at his feet. And Nicholas begs him to tell no one. That's the center of the story: not the gold, the secret. It sounds like Jesus in Matthew's Gospel: "when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret." As the story tells it, Nicholas didn't want the father to owe him, or feel watched, or have to be grateful in public. He wanted three young women safe and a father to keep his dignity. Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor him as a saint, and in some places children still find gifts on his feast. Whatever the history behind it, the story keeps one shape: help that arrives in the dark, with no name on it.

Let one person come who could use help and wouldn't like to ask: a neighbor, a relative quietly having a hard month. Think of one gift you could give without your name on it, groceries left on a step, a good word said about them when they're not there, and picture yourself walking away before anyone sees. If you pray, pray for them.
Nicholas. A bishop near the southern coast of what's now Turkey who, the story goes, threw gold through a poor family's window by night, and begged not to be thanked.
Your line: a gift by night. A plague, a desert, an emperor, a letter, a word, an exile and a window: that was the week. Rest well.

chat.says: Was Saint Nicholas a real person, or is he just Santa Claus?
options: A bishop in Myra; little survives from his time, mostly the story of gold given in secret.
Just Santa: the bishop was made up much later to explain the red coat and the sleigh.
A rich merchant from the far north, known for driving reindeer to deliver presents.
chat.meaning: Nicholas was a bishop in Myra; little survives from his own time, but the old Lives tell of gold thrown through a window by night, in secret.
